panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Patient CT showing systemic-sclerosis-associated fibrotic NSIP-pattern interstitial lung disease, including ground-glass opacity and traction bronchiectasis. B: Patient mediastinal-window CT showing esophageal dilation and a dilated main pulmonary artery, identified in the caption as a sign of pulmonary hypertension complicating SSc.
panels.attribution_text: Di Maggio et al. Biomarkers in Systemic Sclerosis: An Overview.. Current issues in molecular biology 2023. doi:10.3390/cimb45100490. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A 63-year-old female with the diagnosis of SSc. (A) Axial High-resolution CT scan shows traction bronchiectasis (white arrows) in a back-ground of diffuse ground-glass opacities, related to a fibrotic nonspecific pneumonia (NSIP) patter. (B) Using the mediastinal window setting the dilatation of the main pulmonary artery (32 mm) can also be recognized as sign of pulmonary hypertension, a common complication of the disease. Moreover a dilatation of the esophagus (*) can be seen (operator E.B., Radiology Unit, University of Trieste, University Hospital of Cattinara).
in_text_mentions: ILD, the most common pattern in SSc is NSIP (50-77% of SSc patients with ILD) with bilateral involvement typically starting at the bases. The UIP pattern occurs more rarely during SSc and is characterized by shorter survival than NSIP. SSc-ILD is detected after diagnosis by high resolution CT (HR-CT) and progression by both HR-CT and pulmonary function tests (PFT) (Figure 1) [95,96,97,98]. Studies have shown how quantitative CT scanning can be used to detect early SSc-ILD and differentiate it from interstitial pneumonia and to follow the progression of SSc-ILD more precisely [95,96,97,98,99].

findings.evidence: Caption: reticular, linear, and minor ground-glass opacities in systemic sclerosis-related interstitial lung disease.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Patient HRCT demonstrating SSc-associated interstitial lung disease with reticular, linear, and minor ground-glass opacities. B: Patient HRCT showing peripheral basal ground-glass opacities characteristic of SSc-associated interstitial lung disease. C: Patient HRCT showing diffuse ground-glass and reticular abnormalities with septal thickening involving the basal lower lobes in SSc-related ILD. D: Patient HRCT showing more extensive SSc-associated ILD with traction bronchiectasis and an additional bulla. E: Patient HRCT showing extensive interstitial opacification and honeycombing in advanced SSc-associated ILD.
panels.attribution_text: Rutka et al. Imaging in Diagnosis of Systemic Sclerosis.. Journal of clinical medicine 2021. doi:10.3390/jcm10020248. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: High-resolution computed tomography scans show different stages of systemic sclerosis-related interstitial lung disease. (A) Reticular, linear, and minor ground glass opacities; (B) ground glass opacities peripherally in the basal parts of the lower lobes; (C) diffuse ground glass, reticular opacities with discreet interlobular septal thickening in the basal parts of the lower lobes; (D) ground glass opacifications with reticular and linear patterns with traction bronchiectasis with an additional bulla; and (E) interstitial opacifications with extensive honeycombing.
in_text_mentions: SSc-ILD shows numerous similarities to non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) both in medical imaging and histopathological examinations [63]. In HRCT (Figure 5) interstitial opacifications are seen in the dorso-basal parts of the lungs—usually of reticular morphology. Ground-glass opacities are also frequent, but typically they spare the subpleural parenchyma [64]. Symptoms that are not as characteristic of SSc but are reported in some of the patients include traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing, although the latter is typical rather in usual interstitial pneumonia than in NSIP [65,66

findings.evidence: Caption identifies subtle subpleural ground-glass opacities at the lung bases suspicious for NSIP in a patient with systemic sclerosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Axial HRCT image from a 43-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis showing subtle subpleural basal ground-glass opacities consistent with SSc-associated interstitial lung disease. b: Prone axial HRCT demonstrates persistent basal ground-glass opacities, supporting true SSc-associated ILD rather than dependent gravitational change. c: Medial-window CT image shows a dilated esophagus, a recognized SSc-related manifestation, highlighted by the arrow.
panels.attribution_text: Ruaro et al. The Relationship between Pulmonary Damage and Peripheral Vascular Manifestations in Systemic Sclerosis Patients.. Pharmaceuticals (Basel, Switzerland) 2021. doi:10.3390/ph14050403. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A 43-year-old female with a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis. Axial high-resolution CT scan obtained in the supine position shows subtle ground-glass opacities in the subpleural regions of the lung bases, suspicious for NSIP (non-specific interstitial pneumonia) (a). When these findings are not prominent, an additional scan can be acquired in the prone position to differentiate ground-glass opacities due to gravitational phenomena from interstitial lung disease. In this patient the ground-glass opacities persist in the prone position, confirming the interstitial lung involvement (b). Additional systemic sclerosis-related findings should be searched for, such as a dilated esophagus on images reconstructed using an appropriate mediastinal window setting (c).
in_text_mentions: ree of reticulation, suggestive of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP). The predominant observations in the basal areas of the lungs are low lung volumes and interstitial reticular thickening. In the late lung involvement stages, pulmonary fibrosis manifests as traction bronchiectasis and honeycomb cysts, a marker for usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) [55,56,57,58,59,60,61,62,63,64] (Figure 1). These two alterations have been observed in up to 33% of SSc-ILD patients, suggesting that these patients may have a mixture (or overlap) of UIP and NSIP patterns [55,56,57,58,59,60,61,62,63,64].

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a human eyelid showing visible telangiectatic vessels. The caption and article context specifically attribute the eyelid manifestation to systemic sclerosis; no cutaneous subtype is directly stated.
panels.attribution_text: Paczwa et al. Ocular Manifestation in Systemic Sclerosis-A Literature Review.. Life (Basel, Switzerland) 2024. doi:10.3390/life14050627. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
in_text_mentions: proliferation leads to the accumulation of the extracellular matrix (mostly type I collagen) in the skin [5]. The fibrosis in the eyelid skin can result in its stiffness, tightness, and lagophthalmos [5,8], which cause decreased eyelid mobility and consequently disturbances in spreading tear film over the ocular surface. Szucs et al. [9], in their study, investigated 102 eyes of 51 SSc patients. They observed pathologies in the eyelids in more than 56% of the study group. Stiffness, tightness, telangiectasia, and blepharitis were the most common findings [9], as shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real axial HRCT from an SSc patient demonstrating a captioned systemic-sclerosis interstitial lung disease pattern. B: Real coronal HRCT reconstruction demonstrating SSc-related fibrotic NSIP and associated airway enlargement. C: The SSc-focused article and caption identify a 37 mm main pulmonary artery as a sign of pulmonary hypertension, a recognized pulmonary manifestation of systemic sclerosis.

panels.figure_caption: (A,B) Parenchymal signs: axial high resolution CT scan shows a fibrotic NSIP pattern due to the presence of diffuse irregular septal thickening (black arrows), bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis on a background of diffuse ground glass opacities. Both lower lobes are symmetrically involved by these alterations. Bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis (white arrows) are better visualized on the MinIP coronal plane reconstruction; (C) Vascular signs: a main pulmonary artery with a diameter greater than 36 mm measured in a scanning plane of its bifurcation is a sign of pulmonary hypertension.
in_text_mentions: Parenchymal signs. There are different forms of pulmonary involvement in SSc. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial CT image from a 56-year-old male with a diagnosis of SSc showing dilated esophagus with an air-fluid level, directly supported by the caption. B: High-resolution CT demonstrates SSc-associated fibrotic NSIP, with diffuse ground-glass opacity and superimposed septal thickening, bronchiectasis, and bronchiolectasis described in the caption. C: Contrast CT shows enlargement of the main pulmonary artery, captioned as a sign of pulmonary hypertension in the SSc article context. The specific pulmonary hypertension finding is not in the provided vocabulary and is proposed.

panels.figure_caption: (A) Esophageal involvement in a 56-year-old male with a diagnosis of SSc. Axial image with a mediastinal window setting shows a dilatation of the esophagus (diameter >1.2 cm) with an air-fluid level (white arrows); (B) Parenchymal signs: axial high resolution CT scan shows a fibrotic NSIP pattern due to the presence of diffuse irregular septal thickening, bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis on a background of diffuse ground glass opacities (white arrows); (C) Vascular signs: a main pulmonary artery with a diameter greater than 36 mm measured in a scanning plane of its bifurcation is a sign of pulmonary hypertension.
in_text_mentions: ymmetrical distribution; when fibrotic changes occur (fibrotic NSIP pattern), irregular septal thickening, bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis can be recognized on HRCT as superimposed features on a background of pre-existing ground glass opacities [43]. The usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern is less common in SSc and this pattern is characterized by the presence of irregular septal thickening in the peripheral and subpleural regions of the lungs, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis and pulmonary volume loss. This pattern has a worst prognosis and a faster progression [3] (Figure 3).
